metadata.title: Who will be the AI trade's real winners: The makers vs. the takers?

content.text:
00:00 Speaker A
Samsung itself kind of following the playbook of doing great, but not great enough. I mean, you know, again, like it's almost blasé at this point how good the numbers are. And this is preliminary numbers from um from Samsung. Revenue more than doubling, um the company's um implied margins. They didn't um report the actual margins, but you can sort of imply. Counterpoint said that if you look at the three memory chip makers, they were 75% to 80% margin in this quarter, which is incredible. And yet the stock is down.
00:43 Speaker B
One of my themes at you know, that and I I said this on on record at different couple places yesterday, what is my big fear for this earning season is not that these companies won't do phenomenally. They did. But that the market set the bar too high.
01:06 Speaker C
Deutsche Bank had written that you they only beat profit expectations by 6%, only. So you saw some selling uh after that print. But look, there's been some nervousness in the market about this because you have these sky high prices. You have somebody that's buying that on the other end. So you've got companies that are buying that. How much productivity are they getting from this AI? So there's these concerns that are bubbling up under the surface about these memory prices.
01:34 Speaker B
One of my themes has been sort of makers versus takers. The the makers, you know, the the makers being the the the semiconductors, the the picks and shovels of this gold rush. The takers, which were the favorite stocks or, you know, let's say the AI hyperscalers and friends. At some point, there's a limit to how much suppliers can squeeze their best customers before their best customers say, you know what, maybe this isn't working for us at this price. Maybe we maybe we can't buy this much. Meta tapped out last week. I think that I think that was a little bit lost on the market was that meta basically said, we're no longer building anymore. By the way, if you guys want to take some of our excess capacity off our hands, by all means, go ahead. What happens if, you know, a Microsoft or or an Alphabet says, you know what, we've spent bucket loads on this stuff. Right. Maybe we're going to take a little bit of a break. Maybe we're not going to maybe we'll just keep spending at the current pace. We're not going to expand at the levels that you guys are expecting us to, especially because the more they they have to spend more just to just to run in place because if the prices keep going, yes, and and to your point in as they do have long-term supplier relationships, so the prices aren't going up as fast as let's say um the non-locked-in price bars are. But but they're getting they're spending more and effectively getting less. That's not a great argument.
